readings.title: Alice: the opening poem, “All in the golden afternoon”
readings.challenge: Picture a real afternoon from small clues, and work out who the three listeners are.
readings.focus: Carroll remembers the boat trip on which the story of Wonderland was first told.
readings.context: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson (1832–1898), a mathematics teacher at Oxford University. He first made up this story on a boat trip in 1862 for three sisters, Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell, and published it as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865; this printing has pictures by Arthur Rackham. This poem opens the book. The “cruel Three” are the three sisters; Prima, Secunda and Tertia are Latin for First, Second and Third. Oars are “plied” when they are worked; an edict is an order; “anon” means soon; a pilgrim is a traveller to a holy place, who might bring home a wreath of flowers to remember it.

excerpt.locator: The prefatory poem “All in the golden afternoon,” complete; opens “All in the golden afternoon Full leisurely we glide; For both our oars, with little…”; closes “…mystic band, Like pilgrim's wither'd wreath of flowers Pluck'd in a far-off land.”.

questions.prompt: Who is rowing the boat, and how well? Find the lines that tell you.
facilitatorNotes: The children are: “little arms” work the oars “with little skill,” and “little hands” only pretend to steer. The boat drifts slowly, which fits a lazy, golden afternoon.
evidence: For both our oars, with little skill,
By little arms are plied,

questions.prompt: What does each of the three sisters want from the storyteller?
facilitatorNotes: Prima orders him to begin; Secunda hopes there will be nonsense in it; Tertia interrupts about once a minute. Three different listeners, three different demands.
evidence: Her edict "to begin it"—
"There will be nonsense in it!"—
While Tertia interrupts the tale

questions.prompt: When the tired storyteller tries to stop, what do the children cry? Why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: He says “The rest next time—” and they answer “It is next time!” They will not let him stop, which is how the long story grew one piece at a time.
evidence: "The rest next time—" "It is next time!"

questions.prompt: In the last stanza Carroll calls the story a “wither’d wreath of flowers.” What does he hope Alice will do with it? Why might he call it withered?
facilitatorNotes: He hopes she will keep it gently among her memories of childhood. Withered flowers are kept to remember a journey after it is over; the golden afternoon is past, but the story keeps it. Some readers hear a little sadness about growing up.
evidence: Lay it where Childhood's dreams are twined
Like pilgrim's wither'd wreath of flowers

readings.title: Alice, chapter I, part 1: Down the rabbit-hole
readings.challenge: Follow Alice’s thoughts as she talks to herself, and notice the narrator’s jokes in brackets.
readings.focus: A bored girl follows a rabbit with a watch and falls into a world where odd things seem natural.
readings.context: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson (1832–1898), a mathematics teacher at Oxford University. He first made up this story on a boat trip in 1862 for three sisters, Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell, and published it as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865; this printing has pictures by Arthur Rackham. This is the first chapter. A waistcoat is a vest; marmalade is orange jam; latitude and longitude are lines on a map; Alice means the Antipodes, places on the opposite side of the earth, but gets the word wrong; to curtsey is to bob down politely.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Down the Rabbit-Hole,” from the beginning through the end of the fall; opens “ALICE was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having…”; closes “…thump! thump! down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Alice bored at the start? What does she think a book needs?
facilitatorNotes: Her sister’s book has no pictures or conversations, which Alice thinks are the whole use of a book. This book, the reader may notice, has plenty of both.
evidence: "and what is the use of a book," thought Alice, "without pictures or conversations?"

questions.prompt: What did not surprise Alice about the White Rabbit, and what finally made her jump up and chase it?
facilitatorNotes: Hearing it talk seemed natural at the time; seeing it take a watch out of a waistcoat-pocket did not. The narrator says she should have wondered at the talking too.
evidence: nor did Alice think it so very much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself,
the Rabbit actually took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket,

questions.prompt: What does Alice do with the empty marmalade jar, and why? What does that show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She puts it back in a cupboard as she falls, so as not to drop it on somebody below. She stays careful and polite even in the strangest moment.
evidence: she did not like to drop the jar for fear of killing somebody underneath,

questions.prompt: As she grows sleepy, “Do cats eat bats?” turns into “Do bats eat cats?” Why does the narrator say it “didn't much matter which way she put it”?
facilitatorNotes: She cannot answer either question, so turning it round makes no difference to her. The swap also shows her mind drifting into a dream.
evidence: as she couldn't answer either question, it didn't much matter which way she put it.

readings.title: Alice, chapter I, part 2: A golden key and DRINK ME
readings.challenge: Keep track of the key, the door and the bottle, and enjoy the narrator’s joking “rules.”
readings.focus: Alice finds a way into a lovely garden but is the wrong size for it.
readings.context: Recap: Alice followed a White Rabbit with a watch down a rabbit-hole and fell for a long time, talking to herself about her cat, Dinah, until she landed on a heap of sticks and leaves. A telescope folds up into itself when it is shut.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, from her landing to her shrinking to ten inches high, ending “for she could not remember ever having seen such a thing”; opens “Alice was not a bit hurt, and she jumped up on to her feet in a moment: she looked up,…”; closes “…after the candle is blown out, for she could not remember ever having seen such a thing.”.

questions.prompt: What does Alice find on the glass table, and what does it open?
facilitatorNotes: A tiny golden key, which fits a little door about fifteen inches high hidden behind a curtain. Through it she sees “the loveliest garden you ever saw.”
evidence: there was nothing on it but a tiny golden key,
behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high:

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t Alice drink from the bottle at once? What “rules” does she remember?
facilitatorNotes: She checks that it is not marked “poison,” remembering stories of children who forgot simple rules: red-hot pokers burn, deep cuts bleed, poison disagrees with you. The narrator is joking: the rules are so obvious that they are funny.
evidence: see whether it's marked 'poison' or not;
it is almost certain to disagree with you, sooner or later.

questions.prompt: What does the drink taste like? What is funny about the list?
facilitatorNotes: Cherry-tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey, coffee and hot buttered toast: sweet and savoury favourites all at once, which no real drink could taste like.
evidence: a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pineapple, roast turkey, coffee, and hot buttered toast,

questions.prompt: Why does Alice wait a few minutes after she shrinks? What worries her?
facilitatorNotes: She fears she might keep shrinking until she goes out “like a candle.” Then she tries to imagine a candle flame after it is blown out, which is impossible: Carroll enjoys questions with no answer.
evidence: in my going out altogether, like a candle.
she tried to fancy what the flame of a candle looks like after the candle is blown out,

readings.title: Alice, chapters I–II: EAT ME, and curiouser and curiouser
readings.challenge: Follow Alice’s reasoning about the cake, and notice how she talks to herself as if she were two people.
readings.focus: Alice tries to solve her problem by logic, and the answer goes wrong in a new way.
readings.context: Recap: underground, Alice found a tiny door into a lovely garden and a little golden key that fits it. A bottle labelled “DRINK ME” shrank her to ten inches high, just right for the door. To box someone’s ears is to slap them; croquet is a lawn game played with mallets and balls; a carrier delivered parcels; “Esq.” is a polite title once written after a man’s name; a fender is a low guard in front of a fireplace; kid gloves are made of soft goatskin.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, from the forgotten key to the end, and Chapter II, “Pool of Tears,” to the White Rabbit’s flight; opens “After a while, finding that nothing more happened, she decided on going into the garden…”; closes “…white kid gloves and the fan, and scurried away into the darkness as hard as he could go.”.

questions.prompt: What went wrong once Alice was small enough for the door?
facilitatorNotes: She had left the key on the glass table and could not climb its slippery leg to reach it, so she sat down and cried.
evidence: she found she had forgotten the little golden key,
the poor little thing sat down and cried.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator tell us about the advice Alice gives herself?
facilitatorNotes: She gives herself very good advice but seldom follows it; she sometimes scolds herself to tears, and once boxed her own ears for cheating herself at croquet. She likes pretending to be two people.
evidence: She generally gave herself very good advice (though she very seldom followed it),
this curious child was very fond of pretending to be two people.

questions.prompt: Before eating the cake, Alice decides she will get into the garden whatever happens. Explain her reasoning. Does it work?
facilitatorNotes: Larger, she can reach the key; smaller, she can creep under the door. Sensible, but it fails: she grows to over nine feet, gets the key, and is now far too big for the door.
evidence: if it makes me grow larger, I can reach the key; and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door;

questions.prompt: “Curiouser and curiouser!” is not good English. Why does Alice say it? What other nonsense does she talk to her feet?
facilitatorNotes: She is so surprised that she forgets how to speak properly. She says goodbye to her feet, now far away, and plans to post them boots at Christmas, addressed to “Alice’s Right Foot, Esq.” Then she admits it is nonsense.
evidence: she was so much surprised, that for a moment she quite forgot how to speak good English
Alice's Right Foot, Esq.

readings.title: Alice, chapter II, part 2: Who in the world am I?
readings.challenge: Watch Alice test her own memory, and hear what is wrong with what she recites.
readings.focus: After so many changes, Alice wonders whether she is still herself.
readings.context: Recap: in the underground hall Alice has shrunk and grown so much that she is now nine feet tall, far too big for the little door to the garden, and has cried a great pool of tears. The White Rabbit ran past and dropped his gloves and fan when she spoke to him. Ringlets are long curls; to signify is to matter. Children of Carroll’s time learned a poem beginning “How doth the little busy bee,” which praises a hard-working bee; Alice’s version goes wrong.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, from “Alice took up the fan and gloves” to her escape from shrinking away altogether; opens “Alice took up the fan and gloves, and, as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself…”; closes “…"for I never was so small as this before, never! And I declare it's too bad, that it is!"”.

questions.prompt: Alice wonders if she was changed in the night. How does she test whether she is still herself?
facilitatorNotes: She compares herself with friends (she cannot be Ada, whose hair is curly) and tests what she knows: times tables, geography, a poem she learned.
evidence: was I the same when I got up this morning?
I'll try if I know all the things I used to know.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong with her times tables and her geography? Say them aloud.
facilitatorNotes: “Four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen”; “London is the capital of Paris.” Everything comes out wrong, so she decides she must have become Mabel.
evidence: four times five is twelve, and four times six is thirteen,
London is the capital of Paris,

questions.prompt: Her poem comes out about a crocodile. What seems friendly about him, and what is he really doing?
facilitatorNotes: He grins cheerfully, spreads his claws neatly and “welcomes little fishes in, / With gently smiling jaws”: he is eating them. The polite words hide a meal. The poem she meant to say praised a busy bee.
evidence: How cheerfully he seems to grin,
And welcomes little fishes in,

questions.prompt: If she is Mabel, Alice says she will stay down here. What would she say to people calling her? What do her last words show she really feels?
facilitatorNotes: She would ask “Who am I then?” and only come up if she liked being that person. But then she bursts into tears and wishes they would call: she is lonely and tired of being alone.
evidence: Who am I then? Tell me that first,
I am so very tired of being all alone here!

readings.title: Alice, chapter II, part 3: The pool and the Mouse
readings.challenge: Notice each time Alice forgets who she is talking to.
readings.focus: Alice tries to make friends with a Mouse, and keeps saying exactly the wrong thing.
readings.context: Recap: Alice has grown huge and shrunk small again in the underground hall; while she was nine feet tall she cried a great pool of tears. Holding the White Rabbit’s fan made her shrink to about two feet. Bathing machines were huts on wheels rolled into the sea for bathers to change in. William the Conqueror invaded England from France in 1066. “Où est ma chatte?” is French for “Where is my cat?” A terrier is a small dog bred to catch rats.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, from her fall into the salt water to the end of the chapter; opens “As she said these words her foot slipped, and in another moment, splash! she was up to…”; closes “…other curious creatures. Alice led the way, and the whole party swam to the shore.”.

questions.prompt: Where does Alice think she has fallen at first? How does she find out the truth?
facilitatorNotes: Into the sea, so she could go home by railway, since every English beach she knows has a station behind it. Then she realizes it is the pool of tears she cried when she was nine feet tall.
evidence: Her first idea was that she had somehow fallen into the sea,
she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high.

questions.prompt: Why does Alice say “O Mouse!”? Where did she get the idea?
facilitatorNotes: From her brother’s Latin grammar book, which lists “O mouse!” as the form for speaking to a mouse. She is trying to be correct and polite.
evidence: A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!

questions.prompt: Alice upsets the Mouse twice. What does she talk about each time, and why does it upset him?
facilitatorNotes: First cats (her French sentence, then Dinah “catching mice”), then a terrier that “kills all the rats.” She keeps forgetting that she is talking to a mouse.
evidence: she's such a capital one for catching mice
He says it kills all the rats and—oh dear!

questions.prompt: Is Alice being unkind to the Mouse? Use what she says and does to decide.
facilitatorNotes: She does not mean harm: she apologizes, tries to change the subject and calls him back gently. But she keeps forgetting how things look to him. Readers may call her thoughtless, kind, or both.
evidence: Oh, I beg your pardon!
Mouse dear! Do come back again,

readings.title: Alice, chapter III, part 1: The driest thing, and a Caucus-race
readings.challenge: Catch the jokes that come from words with two meanings.
readings.focus: A soaking-wet crowd tries two silly ways of getting dry.
readings.context: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson (1832–1898), a mathematics teacher at Oxford University. He first made up this story on a boat trip in 1862 for three sisters, Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell, and published it as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865; this printing has pictures by Arthur Rackham. Alice has fallen into a strange world under the ground and cried a pool of tears. She has swum ashore with a Mouse and a crowd of creatures that fell in: a Duck, a Dodo (a large bird that no longer exists), a Lory (a kind of parrot), an Eaglet (a young eagle) and others. The Mouse reads from a real history lesson about William the Conqueror. To adjourn a meeting is to end it for now; a caucus is a political meeting.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “A Caucus-race and a Long Tale,” from the beginning through the end of the race; opens “THEY were indeed a queer-looking party that assembled on the bank—the birds with draggled…”; closes “…"The race is over!" and they all crowded round it, panting, and asking "But who has won?"”.

questions.prompt: What does the Lory say to win its argument with Alice? Why won’t Alice accept it?
facilitatorNotes: “I am older than you, and must know better.” Alice will not agree without knowing its age, and the Lory refuses to tell. Readers can decide whether being older really makes someone right.
evidence: I am older than you, and must know better;
the Lory positively refused to tell its age,

questions.prompt: The Mouse calls its history lesson “the driest thing I know.” What two meanings of “dry” are mixed up?
facilitatorNotes: Dry can mean dull and boring, or not wet. The Mouse hopes a boring lesson will dry them off, and of course it does not.
evidence: This is the driest thing I know.

questions.prompt: The Duck and the Mouse disagree about the word “it.” What does the Duck think “found it” means?
facilitatorNotes: The Duck thinks “it” must be a thing you find, “a frog or a worm,” so it asks what the archbishop found. In “found it advisable,” “it” does not name a thing at all. The Duck is being literal.
evidence: it's generally a frog or a worm.
The question is, what did the archbishop find?

questions.prompt: How does the Caucus-race work? Why is it hard to tell who has won?
facilitatorNotes: The course is a rough circle, there is no start signal, and everyone runs and stops when they like. With no start and no finish line, there is no way to know who won; the race only ends when they are dry.
evidence: they began running when they liked, and left off when they liked,
But who has won?

readings.title: Alice, chapter III, part 2: Prizes, a long tale, and Dinah
readings.challenge: Hear how one word can sound like another, and follow how a party falls apart.
readings.focus: Alice’s misunderstandings drive off the Mouse, and her talk of Dinah empties the shore.
readings.context: Recap: Alice and a wet crowd of birds and animals tried to get dry, first by listening to the Mouse’s dull history lesson, then by running a Caucus-race in which everyone started and stopped when they liked. Now the Dodo must decide who has won. Comfits are small sweets; a thimble protects a finger when sewing; a cur is a mean dog; to prosecute is to accuse someone in court; pretexts are made-up excuses.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, from the Dodo’s judgment to the end of the chapter; opens “This question the Dodo could not answer without a great deal of thought, and it stood for…”; closes “…half hoping that the Mouse had changed his mind, and was coming back to finish his story.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Dodo decide who has won? Who provides the prizes, and what is odd about Alice’s own prize?
facilitatorNotes: “Everybody has won, and all must have prizes,” paid for by Alice: one comfit each. Her own prize is her own thimble, solemnly handed back to her. Alice thinks it absurd but does not dare laugh.
evidence: Everybody has won, and all must have prizes.
We beg your acceptance of this elegant thimble;

questions.prompt: Alice hears “tale” as “tail.” What story does the Mouse tell, and is the trial in it fair?
facilitatorNotes: Fury, a dog, tells a mouse they will go to court; when the mouse says a trial with no judge or jury is a waste of breath, Fury says he will be both, and condemn the mouse to death. It is not fair at all, which explains why the Mouse hates dogs. The lines get shorter and shorter, like a tail narrowing to its tip.
evidence: It is a long tail, certainly,
'I'll be judge, I'll be jury,'

questions.prompt: “I had not!” cries the Mouse. What does Alice hear, and why does the Mouse walk away?
facilitatorNotes: She hears “a knot!” and offers to help undo it. The Mouse thinks she is making fun of him with nonsense. Alice meant to help, but she has not been listening.
evidence: always ready to make herself useful,
You insult me by talking such nonsense!

questions.prompt: What does Alice say that sends everyone home? Why does she end up crying?
facilitatorNotes: She boasts that Dinah catches mice and will “eat a little bird as soon as look at it.” The birds make excuses and leave. She is left alone, missing Dinah, and feels lonely.
evidence: she'll eat a little bird as soon as look at it!
On various pretexts they all moved off,

readings.title: Alice, chapter IV, part 1: Mary Ann, and a house too small
readings.challenge: Notice how Alice is ordered about, and how she reasons about another strange bottle.
readings.focus: Mistaken for a servant, Alice grows until she fills a whole house.
readings.context: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson (1832–1898), a mathematics teacher at Oxford University. He first made up this story on a boat trip in 1862 for three sisters, Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell, and published it as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865; this printing has pictures by Arthur Rackham. Alice has fallen into a strange world under the ground, where eating and drinking change her size, and she is very small just now. A crowd of animals has just left her alone after she talked too much about her cat, Dinah. Earlier she had picked up the White Rabbit’s fan and gloves, but lost them. A housemaid was a servant who cleaned a house; to be executed is to be put to death as a punishment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Rabbit sends in a Little Bill,” from the beginning until she stops growing; opens “IT was the White Rabbit, trotting slowly back again, and looking anxiously about as it…”; closes “…no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.”.

questions.prompt: Who does the Rabbit think Alice is? Why doesn’t she explain his mistake?
facilitatorNotes: Mary Ann, his housemaid. She is so frightened that she runs off at once to do as he says.
evidence: Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here?
Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once

questions.prompt: Alice imagines Dinah sending her on messages. What is the joke?
facilitatorNotes: Usually people give pets orders. Here a rabbit orders Alice about, so she imagines her own cat doing the same, and decides nobody would let a cat give orders in the house.
evidence: I suppose Dinah'll be sending me on messages next!

questions.prompt: This bottle has no “DRINK ME” label. Why does Alice drink anyway? Is her reason a good one?
facilitatorNotes: Because something interesting always happens when she eats or drinks, and she hopes to grow large. It is a curious reason more than a safe one; in Chapter I she checked for “poison” first.
evidence: I know something interesting is sure to happen,
I do hope it will make me grow large again,

questions.prompt: Describe Alice’s position when she finally stops growing. How does the narrator make it funny as well as frightening?
facilitatorNotes: She lies on the floor with one elbow against the door, one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney. The narrator gives the exact silly details, and Alice’s “Now I can do no more, whatever happens” sounds both brave and comic.
evidence: she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney,
Now I can do no more, whatever happens.

readings.title: Alice, chapter IV, part 2: Pat, Bill and the chimney
readings.challenge: Work out what is happening outside from sounds alone, as Alice must.
readings.focus: Stuck inside the house, Alice argues with herself and fights off the Rabbit’s helpers.
readings.context: Recap: mistaken for the White Rabbit’s housemaid, Mary Ann, Alice went into his house to fetch his gloves and fan, drank from a bottle, and grew until she filled a room, with one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney. A cucumber-frame is a small glass box for growing cucumbers; “yer honour” is a respectful way to address a gentleman; slates are roof tiles.
readings.contentNote: Pat the gardener speaks in a comic Irish accent (“arrum”), a stage joke of Carroll’s time. Alice kicks Bill the Lizard up the chimney.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, from “It was much pleasanter at home” to the crowd reviving Bill; opens “"It was much pleasanter at home," thought poor Alice, "when one wasn't always growing…”; closes “…now—Don't choke him—How was it, old fellow? What happened to you? Tell us all about it!"”.

questions.prompt: Alice argues with herself about growing up. What would be good and bad about never getting any older?
facilitatorNotes: Good: she would never be an old woman. Bad: she would always have lessons to learn. Then she answers herself that there is no room for lesson-books in here anyway.
evidence: never to be an old woman—but then—always to have lessons to learn!
making quite a conversation of it altogether;

questions.prompt: Alice says, “There ought to be a book written about me.” Why is that funny for the reader?
facilitatorNotes: We are reading that very book. Alice imagines writing it when she grows up; the joke is that someone already has.
evidence: There ought to be a book written about me, that there ought!

questions.prompt: Alice cannot see outside. Find one thing she hears and what she works out from it.
facilitatorNotes: A shriek, a fall and broken glass tell her the Rabbit may have fallen into a cucumber-frame; voices and a rumble of cart-wheels tell her they have brought ladders; the shouting tells her Bill is being sent down the chimney.
evidence: from which she concluded that it was just possible it had fallen into a cucumber-frame,
Bill's to go down

questions.prompt: “Why, they seem to put everything upon Bill!” How do the others treat Bill? What does Alice do to him, and how do you feel about it?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone passes every job to Bill, a small lizard, including going down the chimney. Alice, who even feels sorry for him, still kicks him straight back up. Readers may laugh, feel sorry for Bill, or both.
evidence: they seem to put everything upon Bill!
she gave one sharp kick,

readings.title: Alice, chapter IV, part 3: Pebbles, cakes and an enormous puppy
readings.challenge: Test Alice’s reasoning, and see how size changes what is dangerous.
readings.focus: Alice escapes the house only to meet a friendly puppy big enough to trample her.
readings.context: Recap: Alice, grown huge inside the White Rabbit’s house, has fought off the Rabbit and his helpers; when Bill the Lizard came down the chimney, she kicked him out again. A Jack-in-the-box is a toy figure that springs out of a box; a barrowful is a wheelbarrow-load; to worry a stick is to shake and bite it; a hookah is a tall pipe in which smoke is drawn through water.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, from Bill’s account of his flight to the end of the chapter; opens “At last came a little feeble, squeaking voice, ("That's Bill," thought Alice,) "Well, I…”; closes “…smoking a long hookah, and taking not the smallest notice of her or of anything else.”.

questions.prompt: How does Bill describe what happened to him? Why is his description funny?
facilitatorNotes: “Something comes at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I goes like a sky-rocket!” He never saw it was Alice’s foot, and his comparisons are bigger than his voice.
evidence: something comes at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I goes like a sky-rocket!

questions.prompt: The pebbles turn into little cakes. Explain Alice’s reasoning before she eats one. Is it good reasoning?
facilitatorNotes: Any cake will change her size; it cannot make her larger, because there is no room; so it must make her smaller. It works, though the middle step is more hope than rule, as “I suppose” admits.
evidence: as it can't possibly make me larger, it must make me smaller, I suppose.

questions.prompt: The puppy is friendly. Why is it still dangerous, and how does Alice manage it?
facilitatorNotes: It is enormous next to her, and could trample her by accident or eat her if hungry. She plays fetch with a stick, dodges behind a thistle, and slips away when it is tired out. She compares it to playing with a cart-horse.
evidence: it was very like having a game of play with a cart-horse,
This seemed to Alice a good opportunity for making her escape;

questions.prompt: The chapter ends on top of a mushroom. What does Alice see, and what do you predict?
facilitatorNotes: A large blue caterpillar sitting with its arms folded, smoking a hookah and taking no notice of her. Predictions vary: perhaps it will help her, or be rude, or have something to do with changing size.
evidence: a large blue caterpillar, that was sitting on the top with its arms folded,
taking not the smallest notice of her or of anything else.
